raw_plan.interpretation: Read literally: one cold acquisition email, in English, to the selected segment, with a strategy and next action taken from the compiled knowledge. Reader relationship is unknown, so it is written as a first contact: nothing assumed about an installed stack, a cohort date or a past attempt. The dossier narrows fit to cohort-based course operators, so the copy addresses someone running a course or cohort offer who collects student feedback for its sales page — inside the user's selected segment, not a replacement for it. The requested destination stays the self-serve signup; the alternative proposition uses the official support page instead, because it answers its own question without an account.

intent.reason_now: No dated event. The reason to act is structural: follow-up reminders only apply to invites sent after they are switched on, so the order of operations matters before the next batch of invites goes out, not after.
intent.desired_action: Sign up free at app.senja.io/signup and build the invite with follow-ups turned on before sending it.

raw_plan.reader: Someone running a cohort-based course or coaching offer who collects student feedback and puts it on the course or cohort page. Solution_aware: they already know testimonial tools exist and that proof sells a cohort, so the category does not need explaining. The research establishes the reluctance to ask and the uncertainty about how, not a deadline, a platform, a team or a failed previous attempt — treat all of those as unknown.
raw_plan.reader_segment: A course creator or coach who needs student results on camera before the next cohort launch
raw_plan.reader_scope: Qualified scope from the current dossier: cohort-based course operators. Do not generalise the fit to every course creator in the broader map, and do not assert an imminent cohort launch — the research explicitly does not establish that situation.
raw_plan.promise: The repeat ask for student testimonials is something you configure once, not a decision you take again every time — up to three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, only to the students who have not answered.
raw_plan.orientation: Senja is a tool for asking your students for a text or video testimonial and reusing their answers on your course and cohort pages.
raw_plan.arc: Single email, so the whole arc is inside it: name the ask that never gets sent (the second one), turn it into a documented setting with exact numbers, name the order-of-operations catch that makes the setting worth acting on now, then ask for the free account.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: One email was requested, so the only real decision is which single argument to spend it on. Four shelves could carry this campaign: product breadth (21 facts, none strong enough to lead), display and reuse (widgets, reels, Wall of Love), commercial terms (price, the 15-testimonial Free limit), and the asking mechanism. The asking mechanism wins because it is the one tied to a verified problem for this exact reader — P1 (does not know how to get them, does not want to seem pushy) and P3 (praise does not become a testimonial unless you ask, and ask promptly) — and because the previous campaign's rework note identified precisely this: the ask that produces the testimonial is usually the second one, and the second ask is a setting rather than a question of nerve. Display and reuse is the better-stocked shelf but answers a question this reader has not reached; pricing is checkable but leads with a cost before a reason. The objection assigned is the one the verified material actually supports — reminders landing on students they have a relationship with — and it has a bounded, documented answer in E27 (three, at 1/3/7 days, only to non-responders). What it does not have, and what the email must not supply, is evidence that students perceive this as non-pushy or that timely asks yield stronger testimonials; both are explicitly unsupported, so the copy argues from the mechanism and the control, never from the reaction. No proof shelf exists at all — no named customer, no quote, no outcome — so the email asks the reader to test rather than believe, which is also why the self-serve signup is the honest destination for the primary bet.

emails.selection_reason: This reader's verified blocker is not the display of testimonials, it is sending the ask — and specifically sending it twice. Senja documents the second and third ask as a bounded setting on the invite (three emails, 1/3/7 days, non-responders only) with a hard prerequisite: it only applies to invites sent after the switch is on. That makes the useful next decision immediate and concrete for someone with a cohort to invite, and it is supported without needing a customer result, a named reference or a claim about how students react.
emails.target_need: A repeatable, reward-backed ask that produces student video and text proof with results in it, and turns it into page sections, reels and images for the launch
emails.job: Get a cohort course operator to create a free Senja account and set up their student testimonial invite with follow-ups switched on before the invites go out.
emails.single_idea: The ask that gets answered is usually the second one, and in Senja the second ask is a setting rather than a decision: switch follow-ups on and up to three reminders go out 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, to the students who have not answered — but only on invites you send after the switch is on, so the order matters.
emails.felt_need: "I know student proof is what sells the next cohort. I just don't know how to get it without feeling like I'm nagging people — and I'm definitely not sending a third message to someone who ignored the first two." (P1, P3 — verified, single-source)
emails.status_quo: Observed among creators collecting student feedback for course and cohort pages: asking by hand and in person — a message after the programme, a feedback form at the end of a chapter — with any chasing done one message at a time. Write this at audience level or conditionally ("if you're asking one by one"); the research does not establish this recipient's own workflow, tooling or platform.
emails.why_it_fails: When the ask is hand-sent, every reminder is a fresh decision, and the verified problem is that praise does not turn into a testimonial unless someone asks, and asking late gets a weaker answer. So the ask that would have worked is the one that depends on remembering and on being willing to send it again. Keep this about the burden of the approach, never about the reader's diligence or nerve.
emails.mechanism: Follow-ups are a toggle on the invite, not a second email you have to write and decide to send. Turn them on and Senja sends up to three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, and only to students who haven't responded yet. The catch is the whole reason to do this before the next batch goes out: follow-ups only apply to invites sent after you turn them on — students invited before that get no reminders at all. The condition on the payoff is simply having a Senja account and the invite set up there: you verify your email, give your name, website and plan choice, and you can start on Free.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: A different reason to act, aimed at the other verified problem: this creator is unsure whether to ask for video or writing, and where to collect it. The question-type setting and the default consent page answer that mechanically, and Senja's own support page shows both before the reader creates anything — which is the right first ask for a cold reader whose question is 'what does this actually ask my students to do'.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: You don't have to decide between video and written testimonials in the abstract — you decide it per question: set a question to Video and the student has to record or upload; set it to Video and text and they pick one format for that question. Either way it's one personalised page, no account and no software on their side, and Senja puts it at about 30 seconds.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: "Do I ask for video testimonials or just written ones? And where do I even collect them?" (P2 — verified, single-source)
alternative_arguments.status_quo: Collecting student feedback wherever it lands — a form at the end of a module, replies in a chat channel, praise in a DM — and then deciding case by case what to do with it. Keep conditional; it is audience-level observation, not this reader's confirmed setup.
alternative_arguments.why_it_fails: Asking for whatever a student feels like giving leaves the format decision to the person least invested in it, and a written line and a recorded clip are not interchangeable on a cohort page.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: The format is a per-question setting, not a request you make in words: Video forces a recording, Video and text lets the student choose one format for that question, and a student can't submit both to the same question. The consent page is on by default, so the student chooses public or private use as part of submitting — the decision about publishing is made by them, at the moment they answer.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: asking for video is asking a student for a favour that involves effort and exposure, so it feels like the bigger ask. After: it's a question setting on a page that needs no account or software, and the student chooses public or private before you ever see it.
must_not_say: Which format performs better with prospective students — the material does not establish it, and P2 is explicitly off-limits as a solved problem
That students will find a video request comfortable, or that they will respond at all
Anything about the 30-second figure other than that Senja describes it that way — it is unattributed and approximate
That a student can give both a video and written answer to the same question; they cannot
Conversion-rate or enrolment effects of any format
alternative_arguments.objection: "If I set a question to Video, the students who won't film themselves just drop out of the form entirely."
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: See how the question types and the consent page work before you build anything
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Whether to ask their next cohort for video, for text, or to let each student pick — decidable from the documented question settings and the consent default, without creating an account first.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The support page shows the three question settings in the sidebar, the rule that one question takes one format, and that the consent page is on by default so customers choose public or private use. Read-only: nothing to sign up for, nothing to configure.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: Reading the page does not build the form, does not tell them how many testimonials their plan lets them keep visible, and does not establish how their own students will respond.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead with the question they actually asked — video or written — and signal that the answer is a setting, not an opinion. No curiosity gap; this reader is solution_aware and will open a subject that names the decision.

That asking at the right moment produces stronger, more concrete or more detailed testimonials — P3's quality claim is explicitly unsupported
Auto-collect behaviour: triggers on purchase or course completion, and reminders stopping the moment someone submits, belong to connected-platform auto-collect, not to manual invites
Any named customer, quote, user count, '20,000 creators', or any before-and-after — no proof shelf exists for this campaign
A cohort date, cohort size, student count, course platform, or a previous attempt that failed — all unknown about this reader
Widget styles, Wall of Love, Create Reels, the case study generator, rich snippets, Zapier, the API — this reader is not choosing a display format yet
Plan prices and tier comparisons; the only commercial fact this email needs is that they can start on Free
'Increase your conversion rates' or any revenue or enrolment effect

emails.felt_need: A newly launched course creator reports not knowing how to obtain testimonials and feeling reluctant to ask for reviews because it could seem pushy. Neera reports that praise does not automatically become strong testimonials: asking appropriately and promptly matters, and delayed requests can produce weaker recollections.
emails.mechanism: Follow-ups are a toggle on the invite, not a second email you have to write and decide to send. Turn them on and Senja sends up to three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, and only to students who haven't responded yet. The catch is the whole reason to do this before the next batch goes out: follow-ups only apply to invites sent after you turn them on — students invited before that get no reminders at all. The condition on the payoff is simply having a Senja account and the invite set up there: you verify your email, give your name, website and plan choice, and you can start on Free.
emails.next_step_decision: Whether to run the next cohort's testimonial ask in Senja — with the reminders set once — instead of sending each chase by hand.
emails.next_step_value: Signing up is an email verification, then their name, website and plan choice, and they can start on Free. From there the invite and its follow-up switch exist as settings rather than as messages they have to decide to write.
emails.next_step_limit: Signing up settles none of the following, and the email must not imply otherwise: how their students will react, how many testimonials their plan keeps visible, and whether their course platform can trigger requests automatically — that path needs a connected platform.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: A different reason to act, aimed at the other verified problem: this creator is unsure whether to ask for video or writing, and where to collect it. The question-type setting and the default consent page answer that mechanically, and Senja's own support page shows both before the reader creates anything — which is the right first ask for a cold reader whose question is 'what does this actually ask my students to do'.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: You don't have to decide between video and written testimonials in the abstract — you decide it per question: set a question to Video and the student has to record or upload; set it to Video and text and they pick one format for that question. Either way it's one personalised page, no account and no software on their side, and Senja puts it at about 30 seconds.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: The same creator is unsure whether incentives would seem fake, whether to request video or written testimonials, and where to collect and display them.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: The format is a per-question setting, not a request you make in words: Video forces a recording, Video and text lets the student choose one format for that question, and a student can't submit both to the same question. The consent page is on by default, so the student chooses public or private use as part of submitting — the decision about publishing is made by them, at the moment they answer.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: asking for video is asking a student for a favour that involves effort and exposure, so it feels like the bigger ask. After: it's a question setting on a page that needs no account or software, and the student chooses public or private before you ever see it.
must_not_say: Which format performs better with prospective students — the material does not establish it, and P2 is explicitly off-limits as a solved problem
That students will find a video request comfortable, or that they will respond at all
Anything about the 30-second figure other than that Senja describes it that way — it is unattributed and approximate
That a student can give both a video and written answer to the same question; they cannot
Conversion-rate or enrolment effects of any format
Do not state or imply that every reader uses Form. Present this integration conditionally (for example, 'If you use Form...') unless the user-supplied campaign context establishes it.

Keep the connection route attached to its cited source. A native or prebuilt integration and a custom HTTP/webhook endpoint are separate setup paths unless the source explicitly equates them. A platform name alone establishes neither manual endpoint configuration nor a no-setup connector. Keep unknown setup requirements unknown; do not mix the steps or benefits of those paths.
The product supplies format, collection and display options, but cannot establish which format is best or whether rewards will seem fake; one question cannot receive both text and video.
alternative_arguments.objection: "If I set a question to Video, the students who won't film themselves just drop out of the form entirely."
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Whether to ask their next cohort for video, for text, or to let each student pick — decidable from the documented question settings and the consent default, without creating an account first.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The official page documents this verified fact: Setting a question to Video requires students to record or upload a video; Video and text lets them choose one format.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: Reading the page does not build the form, does not tell them how many testimonials their plan lets them keep visible, and does not establish how their own students will respond.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead with the question they actually asked — video or written — and signal that the answer is a setting, not an opinion. No curiosity gap; this reader is solution_aware and will open a subject that names the decision.
